cards.title: Bundle a want with a need
cards.body: Temptation bundling pairs something you crave with something you should do — so the fun cue pulls the useful habit along. Make the need ride with the want.
cards.source: James Clear · Atomic Habits (via lijubjohn book-notes)

detail.summary: Clear's Make It Attractive lever includes temptation bundling: link an action you want to do with an action you need to do. The dopamine of the want makes the need easier to start — and habit stacking can wire them into a sequence.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body: Willpower is unreliable; attractiveness is not. When you only schedule the hard habit alone, it competes with every more-fun option. Temptation bundling removes that fight by making the useful behavior the gateway to (or companion of) something you already enjoy.

sections.heading: A simple formula
sections.body: After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [HABIT I NEED]. After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]. Example: after I pour coffee, I will review today's top money move for two minutes; after that review, I will open the podcast or show I like. The want is earned by the need — not the other way around.

sections.heading: Try today
sections.body: Pick one sticky need (a 2-minute money check, a short workout opener, or inbox triage) and one guilt-free want (favorite playlist, coffee shop walk, comics). Write the two-line stack once, put it where you'll see it, and run it once today. Adjust the pair if either part feels forced.

bullets: Pair a want (attractive) with a need (useful) so starting is easier
Stack: After current → do need → then get want
Works because the cue for fun also cues the productive action
steps: Name one habit you keep avoiding (the need)
Name one thing you already look forward to (the want)
Write: After X, I will [need]. After [need], I will [want]
Run the stack once today; keep the need tiny so the bundle sticks

cards.title: Inherited India flat/shares: §1014 often steps basis up to FMV
cards.body: US citizens and residents who inherit an India flat, plot, or demat shares generally take a new US tax basis equal to fair market value on the date of death under IRC §1014 — so decades of pre-death appreciation often escape US capital gains when you later sell. Lifetime gifts are different (carryover basis). Separately, aggregate foreign bequests over $100k still need Form 3520 Part IV. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Pub. 551 (12/2025) · IRC §1014 · Gifts from foreign person / Form 3520

detail.summary: When a US citizen or resident inherits property from a decedent, Internal Revenue Code section 1014 generally sets the heir’s initial US tax basis at the property’s fair market value (FMV) on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date if the estate elects it). IRS Publication 551 (revised December 2025), Basis of Assets, restates that rule under “Inherited Property.” For Indian-origin families, that often means an India residential flat, ancestral land, or listed/demat shares that rose for decades while parents held them can reset to current FMV for US tax — shrinking (or wiping out) US capital gain on a later sale compared with using the decedent’s old cost. This tip is educational only and is not tax, legal, or investment advice; facts, India succession law, and India capital-gains/TDS rules can change the picture.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: US citizens and green-card / substantial-presence residents who inherit India real estate, demat equity, mutual-fund units, or other capital assets from parents or other nonresident-alien (or US) decedents. Especially useful when the asset appreciated for years in India and you may sell, gift, or convert currency later. Less relevant if you only received cash (basis issues differ) or if you already sold with well-documented basis.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics (§1014 step-up)
sections.body: Per Pub. 551, your basis in inherited property is generally (1) FMV at the date of death, (2) FMV on the alternate valuation date if elected for estate tax, (3) special-use valuation in limited farm/business cases, or (4) other estate-tax consistent values when Schedule A (Form 8971) applies. FMV is the price willing buyer and seller would agree on with knowledge of the facts. Contrast: property received as a lifetime gift usually takes a carryover basis from the donor (with dual-basis rules when FMV is below donor basis) — so dying with appreciated India property often produces a cleaner US capital-gains result than gifting it during life. When you sell, report the disposition on Form 8949 / Schedule D using that stepped-up basis (converted to USD with a consistent FX method). Holding period for inherited property is generally treated as long-term.

sections.heading: India-angle: flats, demat, and Form 3520
sections.body: India location does not by itself deny the §1014 FMV reset for a US person heir — foreign situs assets still need a US basis for US tax. Practical gap: India stamp duty / circle rates may understate true FMV; keep a contemporaneous appraisal, broker comps, or registered-valuer report dated near death for your US file. India may still tax the sale under domestic capital-gains rules and withhold TDS; US tax then interacts via the Foreign Tax Credit (Form 1116) — a separate analysis. Reporting is not the same as income tax: if aggregate gifts/bequests from a nonresident alien or foreign estate (plus related foreign persons) exceed $100,000 in the year, file Form 3520 Part IV (IRS “Gifts from foreign person”); purported gifts from foreign corporations/partnerships use the lower inflation-adjusted threshold ($20,573 for 2026). True bequests are generally not US income, but missing 3520 can still draw §6039F penalties.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: If you inherited India property in the last few years (or expect to), collect: death certificate / succession papers, a dated FMV snapshot as of the date of death (appraisal or documented comps), demat/broker statements, and any Form 3520 you filed or still need. Store that packet before you list or transfer the asset so your §1014 basis is evidence-backed.

sections.heading: Educational label
sections.body: Educational only — not tax advice. Anti-abuse exceptions (for example, appreciated property you gifted to the decedent within one year of death), community-property / joint-tenancy basis splits, PFIC stock inside India mutual funds, and covered-expatriate §2801 rules can override the simple story. Confirm with a cross-border tax professional before filing or selling.

bullets: IRC §1014 + IRS Pub. 551 (12/2025): inherited property basis is generally FMV at date of death (or alternate valuation if elected).
India flat / land / demat shares inherited by a US person commonly qualify for that FMV reset for US capital-gains basis — document FMV; don’t rely on old purchase cost alone.
Lifetime gifts usually carry over the donor’s basis (different, often worse for appreciated assets) — Pub. 551 “Property Received as a Gift.”
Aggregate foreign bequests/gifts from NRA / foreign estate over $100k → Form 3520 Part IV (IRS Gifts from foreign person); corp/partnership purported gifts $20,573 for 2026.
Sale still reported on Form 8949 / Schedule D; India tax/TDS may need Form 1116 FTC coordination.
Educational only — not tax advice.
steps: List every India (or other foreign) asset you inherited and the date of death.
Assemble FMV evidence as of that date (appraisal, registered valuer, broker comps, demat closing prices) and keep FX notes for USD conversion.
Check whether aggregate foreign gifts/bequests that year exceeded $100k (NRA/estate) and whether Form 3520 Part IV was filed on time.
Before selling, compute tentative US gain using §1014 basis vs. expected sale proceeds; note India TDS / capital-gains and FTC (Form 1116).
If PFIC-prone India mutual funds or closely held Pvt Ltd shares are in the estate, flag Forms 8621 / 5471 separately with your preparer.

cards.title: AgentCore Optimization: recommend from traces, A/B via Gateway
cards.body: Stop guessing prompt fixes. Point AgentCore Recommendations at production OTEL traces + an evaluator (helpfulness, tool selection, etc.), get a system-prompt or tool-description variant, package it as a config bundle, then split live traffic at AgentCore Gateway with p-values before you promote. Preview loop for SAs writing Bedrock agent blogs.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · May 4, 2026 · AgentCore Optimization docs

detail.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Optimization (preview) closes the observe → evaluate → improve loop for production agents. Instead of reading traces by hand and shipping prompt edits blind, you generate Recommendations from AgentCore Observability traces against a chosen evaluator, package the change as an immutable configuration bundle (system prompt, model ID, tool descriptions), validate offline with batch evaluation (or simulated user datasets), then run A/B tests through AgentCore Gateway with online evaluation, confidence intervals, and p-values before promoting the winner. During preview it targets system prompts and tool descriptions for agents on AgentCore Runtime that already use Observability and Evaluations — educational SA pattern, not a production SLA.

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Agent quality drifts daily as models, tools, and user intents shift. The common fix cycle — complaint → skim traces → rewrite prompt → ship — introduces regressions on other sessions. AgentCore Optimization turns that into a data-backed loop SAs can cite in architecture blogs: traces feed recommendations, recommendations become versioned bundles, Gateway splits traffic, Evaluations score both arms with statistical rigor. Pair it with AgentOps pillars (governance, CI/CD, multi-level eval, observability) from the Jun 1, 2026 AgentOps ML Blog.

sections.heading: Recommendations from real traces
sections.body: Call StartRecommendation (type SYSTEM_PROMPT_RECOMMENDATION or TOOL_DESCRIPTION_RECOMMENDATION). Point recommendationConfig at the CloudWatch log group / agent traces, the current system prompt (or tool descriptions), and an evaluationConfig with the reward signal you care about — built-in evaluators such as Builtin.Helpfulness or a custom LLM-as-judge. The service reflects on failure patterns for that evaluator and proposes an optimized variant. Tool-description recommendations sharpen how the model chooses tools without changing tool implementations. You decide what advances to validation.

sections.heading: Configuration bundles vs code changes
sections.body: Bundles are immutable, versioned snapshots keyed by runtime ARN: model ID, system prompt, tool descriptions. Agents read the active bundle dynamically via the AgentCore SDK, so prompt/model swaps are configuration changes — not container redeploys. Use bundle variants on the same Runtime for config-only experiments. For code or framework changes, deploy a second Runtime endpoint and compare via Gateway target-based variants instead.

sections.heading: Validate: batch first, then Gateway A/B
sections.body: Batch evaluation runs the candidate against a curated (or LLM-simulated) dataset and reports aggregate scores so known-good cases do not regress — wire this as a CI gate. Then configure AgentCore Gateway to split live traffic between control and treatment (percentage you set). Online evaluation scores every session; results include confidence intervals and p-values. Promote the winner as the default; pause the test to roll back to the prior configuration. Two variant modes: configuration-bundle variants (same target, W3C baggage injects bundle ref) or target-based variants (different Runtime endpoints).

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: In a non-prod account with AgentCore Runtime + Observability + Evaluations enabled, pick Builtin.Helpfulness (or a custom evaluator), run StartRecommendation on a week of failing sessions, create two config bundles (baseline vs recommendation), run batch eval on your gold prompts, then start a low-percentage Gateway A/B before touching production defaults. Document the loop for your next Bedrock agent blog.

cards.title: Strands harness: open agent stack, ~28% fewer tokens
cards.body: AWS Strands team shipped a fully assembled general-purpose agent harness (Apache 2.0, Sep 21): one line of Python/TypeScript, Bedrock default (also Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/Ollama). Prompt caching + context compaction baked in; team reports ~28% lower token cost vs Claude Code/Codex-class harnesses at similar accuracy. Deploy local or any Linux container (ECS, AgentCore, Cloud Run…).
cards.source: Strands Agents Blog · AWS Weekly Roundup · Sep 21–28, 2026

detail.summary: On Sep 21, 2026 the Strands Agents team released Strands harness: a batteries-included, general-purpose agent harness (not a coding-only IDE agent) under Apache 2.0. One call to create_harness / createHarness wires a model across Amazon Bedrock (default), Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, or LiteLLM. Defaults for prompt caching and context management drove the headline result: about 28% lower token cost than Claude Code, Codex, and similar harnesses on the same Claude/GPT models across six Harbor benchmarks, with equal or better accuracy. AWS Weekly Roundup (Sep 28) amplified it for builders evaluating agent runtimes.

sections.heading: Why it matters this week
sections.body: Recent Bedrock model drops (GPT-6 Sol/Luna, AgentCore Runtime V2) answer which model to call. Strands harness answers how you wrap tools, memory, and context so those models stay cheap and reliable in production. For SA and builder work, it is a concrete open baseline you can run locally, then ship in ECS or Bedrock AgentCore without rewriting the loop.

sections.heading: What ships by default
sections.body: Shell, file read/write/edit, and web tools (primitives models already know). Context management: bulky tool results over ~1500 tokens get truncated/offloaded to files; compaction triggers above ~85% of the context window; recovery runs inside the loop on overflow. Long-term memory across runs via session ID. Built-in helper/subagent for open-ended subtasks plus a checklist/todos tracker. Loads skills when present. Tuned system prompt: explore before changing, confirm before irreversible actions, verify before done.

sections.heading: Cost and accuracy claims
sections.body: On the same Claude or GPT models across six benchmarks (distributed Harbor runs on EC2), Strands harness showed better token efficiency and nearly equal scores vs Claude Code, Codex, and other popular harnesses — about 28% lower cost without trading away accuracy. With Fable 5 they report 77% lower cost than Claude Code and a higher Terminal Bench 2.1 score. Treat vendor benchmarks as directional; re-run on your own tasks before committing a platform.

sections.heading: Where it runs
sections.body: Local laptop, or any Linux container host: Modal, Cloudflare Containers, Azure Container Apps, Google Cloud Run, Amazon ECS, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are called out. Install: pip install strands-harness or npm install @strands-agents/harness. Interactive path: npm install -g @strands-agents/cli, prototype in plain English, then /export to Python or TypeScript.

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: Spin a non-prod Bedrock-backed harness on one research-and-write task you already do manually. Compare tokens and wall time against your current coding-agent loop. If the defaults hold, decide whether AgentCore or ECS is the deploy target — do not rewrite production prompts until you have that baseline.

cards.title: Form 5471: India Pvt Ltd shares can trigger a $10k reporting trap
cards.body: Own (or control) stock in an India private limited company as a US citizen or resident? Form 5471 may be mandatory under IRC §§6038/6046 even when the company paid you nothing — Category 4 if you control >50%, Category 5 if you are a ≥10% US shareholder of a CFC. Miss the attach-to-return deadline and the baseline §6038 penalty is $10,000 per foreign corporation per year. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · About Form 5471 · Instructions for Form 5471 (12/2025) · §§6038/6046

detail.summary: Form 5471 (Information Return of U.S. Persons With Respect To Certain Foreign Corporations) is how certain US citizens and residents who are officers, directors, or shareholders in foreign corporations satisfy the reporting requirements of Internal Revenue Code sections 6038 and 6046. For Indian-origin US residents who founded, inherited, or still hold shares in an India private limited company (or group of related companies), this form is one of the most commonly missed international information returns — and one of the most expensive to miss. The Instructions for Form 5471 (revised December 2025) confirm a $10,000 penalty for each annual accounting period of each foreign corporation for failure to furnish the information required by section 6038(a) within the time prescribed, with additional $10,000 increments after IRS notice (capped) and a separate FTC haircut. Educational only — not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: US citizens and green-card / substantial-presence residents who (1) founded or still own an India Pvt Ltd (startup, consulting firm, family holding company, or operating business), (2) are officers or directors of a foreign corporation when another US person crosses a 10% ownership threshold (Category 2), (3) acquired, disposed of, or became a US person while holding ≥10% (Category 3), (4) control the company — more than 50% of vote or value — as a Category 4 filer, or (5) are a ≥10% US shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation (CFC) as a Category 5 filer. A CFC generally means US shareholders own more than 50% of vote or value on any day of the foreign corporation’s tax year. Family attribution under section 958 can stack siblings/parents/spouse ownership into CFC status even when no single person owns a majority.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Attach a separate Form 5471 (and the schedules your category requires) to your US income tax return and file both by the due date including extensions. Category 4 (control >50% vote or value at any time during your tax year) and Category 5a (US shareholder of a CFC who owned the stock on the last day it was a CFC) are the heavy lifts: they typically pull in Schedules C/F/H/I/I-1/J/M/P/Q/R and can surface Subpart F and GILTI inclusions on your Form 1040 even if the India company never declared a dividend. Category 2/3 focus more on ownership-change reporting via Schedule O. Dormant companies may use the Rev. Proc. 92-70 summary procedure (page 1 only, labeled accordingly) — still a filing, not a free pass. Items reported on Form 5471 generally need not be duplicated on Form 8938 (FATCA), but FBAR (FinCEN 114) is a separate Bank Secrecy Act filing if foreign financial accounts exceed the threshold.

sections.heading: India-angle: Pvt Ltd + family attribution
sections.body: An India private limited company is a foreign corporation for US tax purposes. Typical traps: (1) you left India on H-1B/L-1/green card but kept founder shares or a nominee stake in the old Pvt Ltd; (2) parents/siblings in India hold the rest of the stock and constructive ownership under section 958(b) / section 318 principles pushes you over Category 4 control or makes the company a CFC with you as a Category 5 US shareholder; (3) you are an unpaid director on paper for the family company and a US person acquires ≥10%, triggering Category 2; (4) the company looks dormant (no employees, one bank account) so you assume no US filing — Rev. Proc. 92-70 still wants a labeled summary Form 5471. Separately, if the company is a CFC, Schedule I / Form 8992 territory can produce Subpart F or GILTI income inclusions that are taxable on your US return even when India taxes the company differently and you took no cash. Pair this with last week’s treaty Article 4 and Form 1116 thinking only after the information return is scoped — Form 5471 is disclosure first.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: List every India (or other foreign) corporation where you are a shareholder, officer, or director. For each, jot direct + family-attributed vote and value percentages and whether US persons together own more than 50%. If any Category 2–5 box might apply, calendar Form 5471 with your 2026 return (or extension) and bring the cap table to a cross-border CPA before year-end — do not wait for a K-1-style slip from India, because none will arrive.

bullets: Form 5471 satisfies IRC §§6038 and 6046 reporting for certain US officers, directors, and shareholders of foreign corporations (IRS About Form 5471 / Instructions 12/2025).
Category 4 = control (>50% vote or value); Category 5 = ≥10% US shareholder of a CFC (US shareholders own >50% on any day).

Baseline §6038(a) penalty: $10,000 per foreign corporation per annual accounting period; after IRS 90-day notice, +$10,000 per 30 days (additional capped at $50,000) plus foreign-tax-credit reduction under §6038(c).
India Pvt Ltd founder/family shares + section 958 attribution are a classic miss; dormant entities may still need Rev. Proc. 92-70 summary filing.
Educational only — not tax advice; category tests and CFC/GILTI math are fact-specific.
steps: Inventory foreign corporations (especially India Pvt Ltds) where you are shareholder, officer, or director; note vote/value % including family attribution.
Map yourself to Form 5471 Categories 2–5 using the Instructions for Form 5471 chart; mark CFC status if US shareholders own >50%.
If any category applies, plan Form 5471 + required schedules with your return (or extension) and a cross-border advisor — treat the $10,000-per-entity penalty as the cost of ignoring it.

cards.title: Deep work beats shallow busywork
cards.body: Distraction-free focus creates hard-to-copy value. Shallow tasks feel productive but rarely move the needle — protect depth on purpose.
cards.source: Cal Newport · Deep Work (via mgp book-notes)

detail.summary: Newport's claim: deep work (distraction-free concentration at your cognitive limit) is getting rarer and more valuable. People who make it the core of how they work learn faster and produce things that are hard to copy. Shallow work is logistical, often distracted, and easy to replicate.

sections.heading: What deep work is
sections.body: Deep work is professional activity done with undivided attention — the kind that stretches your skills and creates new value. Shallow work is emailing, coordinating, and other low-cognition tasks you can do while half-distracted. Both exist; only one compounds skill.

sections.heading: Why it matters now
sections.body: Network tools slice attention into slivers, so most knowledge workers lose the habit of depth. That gap is the opportunity: if deep work is rare and valuable, the people who still protect it thrive. You do not need more hours; you need fewer interruptions during the hours that count.

sections.heading: Try today
sections.body: Block one 60–90 minute deep-work window. Pick one hard task (learning, writing, planning money rules — not inbox). Silence notifications, close chat, and treat the block like a meeting with yourself. One protected session beats a day of fragmented busyness.

bullets: Deep work: distraction-free focus that pushes your cognitive limit
Shallow work: easy, logistical, often distracted — low unique value

cards.title: Bedrock prompt caching: put cachePoint where context repeats
cards.body: Same long system prompt, tool schemas, or document across many Converse turns? Drop a cachePoint after the static prefix so later calls read cacheWrite-priced tokens as cheap cache reads (up to ~90% off input on hits). Prefer Converse over InvokeModel for model-agnostic markers; watch TTL and CRIS write churn.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · Sep 15, 2026 · Bedrock User Guide

detail.summary: Amazon Bedrock prompt caching lets you mark reusable prompt prefixes so subsequent Converse (or ConverseStream) requests skip reprocessing that prefix. The Sep 15, 2026 AWS ML Blog walks six Converse patterns: message/document caching, system-prompt caching, tool-definition caching, mixed TTL (1h then 5m), SHA-256 tenant isolation, and LangChain ChatBedrockConverse.create_cache_point(). Explicit caching uses a cachePoint block after static content; implicit caching (where supported) tries prefix reuse without markers. Cache scope is per AWS account and Region. Checkpoints must meet model minimums (for example Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6 often need ≥1,024 tokens before a checkpoint). Default TTL is 5 minutes; many Claude models also support 1h. On hits, cacheReadInputTokens are billed far below standard input; first writes use cacheWriteInputTokens (higher than standard; 1h TTL writes cost more). Educational SA brief — confirm live pricing and model cards before you design for production.

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Agent and RAG apps repeatedly send the same system instructions, tool JSON schemas, and large reference blobs while only the user turn changes. Without caching you pay full input price every hop. Prompt caching is an infrastructure lever: keep prompt quality, cut TTFT on large prefixes, and shrink the input bill on cache hits — without shortening context into a thinner prompt. Pair it with Guardrails for safety; caching does not replace policy controls.

sections.heading: Where to place cachePoint
sections.body: Converse accepts cachePoint in three places, processed tools → system → messages. (1) Messages: put the static document/image blocks, then {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}, then the changing question. (2) System: append cachePoint after a long persona/policy system array. (3) Tools: append cachePoint as the last entry in toolConfig.tools after all toolSpec entries. Claude on Bedrock also supports simplified management: one breakpoint after static content can look back across roughly ~20 prior content blocks for the longest matching prefix.

sections.heading: TTL, CRIS, and metrics
sections.body: Default TTL is 5m; set "ttl": "1h" on supported models for longer sessions (longer TTL checkpoints must appear before shorter ones in the same request). Cross-Region inference profiles can increase cache-write frequency under load — plan for occasional re-writes. Response usage exposes cacheWriteInputTokens and cacheReadInputTokens; with caching enabled, inputTokens is only the non-cached slice. Total input ≈ inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. On ConverseStream, usage often arrives in the terminal metadata event. Log hit ratio; low hits usually mean the prefix mutates or TTL is too short.

sections.heading: Multi-tenant and agent tips
sections.body: Cache entries are account/Region scoped, not tenant scoped. For multi-tenant apps in one account, prepend a SHA-256 of tenant_id to the cached instructions (~16 tokens) so each tenant gets a separate prefix. For agents, cache tool schemas and system instructions once per TTL window; leave real-time user/tool results outside the checkpoint. Prefer Converse cachePoint over InvokeModel’s model-specific cache_control when you want the same code across Claude and Nova. On-demand only — batch inference does not support prompt caching.

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: In a non-prod Region, enable a caching-capable model (e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5), run two Converse calls that share a ≥1,024-token document prefix with a cachePoint between document and question, and confirm request 1 shows cacheWriteInputTokens while request 2 shows cacheReadInputTokens. Then append cachePoint after a realistic toolConfig and measure agent-turn input cost before/after.

bullets: Converse cachePoint after static document / system / tools; dynamic content stays after the marker
Cache hits bill cacheReadInputTokens (~90% lower than standard input per AWS pricing guidance); writes cost more than standard (higher still for 1h TTL)
Meet model minimum tokens per checkpoint (Sonnet 4.5/4.6 often 1,024; some Opus/Haiku tiers differ — check the model card)
TTL default 5m; optional 1h on supported Claude models; order longer TTL before shorter
Account + Region scope; use SHA-256 tenant prefix for isolation in shared accounts
CRIS can increase write churn; monitor cacheWrite vs cacheRead in CloudWatch/app logs
Educational SA pattern — not a cost guarantee; validate against current Bedrock pricing

detail.summary: On Sep 23, 2026 AWS announced native Salesforce and Zendesk data source connectors for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. You hand over instance credentials (OAuth via Secrets Manager); the connector handles crawling, metadata extraction, and incremental sync so RAG apps stay current without a home-grown ingest pipeline. Use cases called out by AWS: customer support bots grounded in Zendesk help + community answers, and internal sales enablement assistants that retrieve Salesforce knowledge articles. Separately, docs warn that starting Sep 30, 2026, creating new Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and Web Crawler connectors on customer-managed knowledge bases is no longer supported—existing ones keep working—so new work that needs those sources should target Managed Knowledge Base.

sections.heading: Why it matters for SA work
sections.body: RAG architecture questions often hinge on whether you build a custom crawler (Lambda + EventBridge + S3 + OpenSearch) or use a managed connector. Native Salesforce/Zendesk connectors shrink operational overhead and map cleanly to Well-Architected reliability and cost trade-offs—especially when the knowledge already lives in those systems of record. The Sep 30 customer-managed cutoff makes Managed KB the default path for new Salesforce (and related) connectors.

sections.heading: What syncs
sections.body: Salesforce: knowledge articles and related CRM content types the connector can crawl (with inclusion/exclusion pattern filters). Zendesk: help center articles (optional attachments) and community posts, optionally scoped by category/section IDs, community topic IDs, and label names. Both support incremental syncs for added, updated, and deleted content after the first full crawl.

sections.heading: Auth and IAM pattern
sections.body: Store OAuth client credentials in AWS Secrets Manager in the same Region as the knowledge base. Salesforce Connected App uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials (consumer key/secret; Run As user configured). Zendesk uses OAuth 2.0 with clientId, clientSecret, and instanceUrl in the secret. Grant the knowledge base IAM role Secrets Manager + connector permissions; prefer least privilege and rotate secrets regularly. Do not reuse one secret across unrelated data sources.

sections.heading: Permissions and PII caveats
sections.body: Anything synced becomes retrievable by principals with bedrock:Retrieve on that knowledge base—including content that had tighter controls in the source system. Zendesk docs note no document-level access control on crawled content. Salesforce crawl can include Case/Contact/Lead fields with personal data—use exclusion filters. Salesforce connector (customer-managed path) notes: preview caveats may apply, no multimodal tables/charts, and historically OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store pairing—confirm current Managed KB store options in the console for your Region.

sections.body: In a non-prod account, create a Managed Knowledge Base, add a Zendesk or Salesforce data source with a Secrets Manager secret pointing at a low-sensitivity sandbox, run one sync, then Retrieve with a few real support/sales questions. Compare latency and answer grounding vs your current PDF/S3 corpus before planning a migration off a custom crawler.

cards.title: India–US treaty Article 4: dual-resident tie-breaker
cards.body: Resident of both India and the US under domestic law (green card + India ROR, or substantial presence + Indian residential status)? Article 4 of the India–US income tax treaty cascades permanent home → centre of vital interests → habitual abode → nationality to assign one treaty residence. Claiming India under the treaty usually means Form 1040-NR + Form 8833 — and the saving clause still lets the US tax its citizens worldwide. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Tax treaties · Form 8833 · India–US treaty Art. 4

detail.summary: If you are a resident of the United States under IRC §7701(b) (green card or substantial presence) and also a resident of India under the Income-tax Act, 1961, you are a dual-resident taxpayer. Article 4 of the Convention between the United States and India for the Avoidance of Double Taxation (signed 1989, in force 1990) supplies a tie-breaker so you are treated as a resident of only one country for treaty purposes. The cascade is: permanent home available → closer personal and economic relations (centre of vital interests) → habitual abode → nationality → mutual agreement of the competent authorities. Dual residents who claim treaty residence of India for US return purposes generally file Form 1040-NR and attach Form 8833 (treaty-based return position). Article 1(3) (the saving clause) still lets the United States tax its citizens — and, subject to narrow exceptions in Article 1(4), its residents — as if the Convention had not come into effect. Educational only — not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin green-card holders and long-stay workers who also meet India’s residential-status tests (for example ordinary resident / resident and ordinarily resident when days in India plus prior-year history stack up), dual homeowners with flats in India and the US, returning NRIs who keep a US green card while rebuilding an India life, and H-1B / L-1 workers who tip into substantial presence while still filing as Indian tax residents. US citizens who are dual residents should model this carefully: the saving clause usually preserves US worldwide taxation even if the tie-breaker points to India.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: First confirm dual residence under each country’s domestic law. Then apply Article 4(2) in order: (a) the Contracting State where you have a permanent home available; if both, the State with which your personal and economic relations are closer (centre of vital interests — family, social ties, occupation, political/cultural activities, place of business, property administration); (b) if that cannot be determined, or you have no permanent home in either State, habitual abode; (c) if habitual abode in both or neither, the State of which you are a national; (d) otherwise the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. If you claim to be a resident of India (not the United States) under the treaty for figuring US income tax, IRS guidance says file a timely Form 1040-NR and attach a fully completed Form 8833 disclosing the treaty-based return position under §6114 / Reg. §301.7701(b)-7. You are treated as a nonresident alien for figuring US tax, while other residency timing rules for alien status can still apply outside that computation.

sections.heading: India-angle: saving clause + what still helps
sections.body: Article 1(3) is the saving clause: notwithstanding most of the Convention, the United States may tax its residents (as determined under Article 4) and, by reason of citizenship, its citizens as if the Convention had not come into effect. Article 1(4) carves back limited benefits (for example certain associated-enterprise adjustments, private pensions/annuities/alimony/child support paragraphs, relief from double taxation, non-discrimination, mutual agreement, plus student/teacher articles for people who are neither citizens nor immigrants of the taxing State). Practically: a US citizen dual resident rarely escapes worldwide US taxation via Article 4 alone; a green-card holder who is not a citizen and whose centre of vital interests clearly sits in India may have a stronger case to claim India treaty residence with Form 8833 — still a facts-and-circumstances call. Either way, keep Form 1116 foreign tax credit and India’s own residential-status rules in the model, and do not confuse treaty residence with immigration status.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: Before year-end planning, list where you have a permanent home available, where your family and main economic ties sit, and your nationality(ies). If you are dual resident and considering an India treaty-residence claim, sketch Form 1040-NR vs Form 1040 outcomes with Form 8833 disclosure, and confirm whether the saving clause blocks the position (especially if you are a US citizen). Bring that one-pager to a cross-border CPA — do not file Form 8833 casually.

bullets: India–US treaty Article 4: dual-resident individuals use a fixed cascade (permanent home → centre of vital interests → habitual abode → nationality → MAP).
Dual resident + claim other country’s treaty residence for US tax → generally Form 1040-NR + Form 8833 (IRS Tax treaties page / About Form 8833).

detail.summary: On Sep 22, 2026 AWS made OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna generally available on Amazon Bedrock, expanding the GPT-6 family alongside Astra. Sol targets recurring complex work (coding, debug, multistep tools); Luna targets high-volume focused tasks (extraction, summarization, classification, routing) with adjustable reasoning effort. cards.title: NRA spouse election: file jointly under §6013(g)
cards.body: Married to someone who is still a nonresident alien for US tax (common India↔US couples)? You can elect to treat the NRA spouse as a US resident for income tax, unlock MFJ brackets/credits, and report worldwide income together. Once-in-a-lifetime choice — model India income + treaty tradeoffs first. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Nonresident spouse · Pub. 519 · IRC §6013(g)

detail.summary: If at year-end one spouse is a US citizen or resident alien (IRC §7701(b)) and the other is a nonresident alien, IRC §6013(g) lets the couple choose to treat the nonresident spouse as a US resident for federal income tax. The election year requires a joint Form 1040; both spouses then report worldwide income for every later year the choice stays in effect (joint or separate returns allowed after year one). Forms 1040/1040-SR now have a Filing Status checkbox for this choice, plus a signed statement. The election is powerful for mixed-status India–US households (citizen/LPR + spouse still NRA under green-card/substantial-presence tests), but it is generally once-in-a-lifetime if ended, pulls India-source income onto the US return, and usually blocks claiming foreign-country residence treaty benefits while it runs. Educational only — not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin US citizens and resident aliens married to a spouse who fails both the green card and substantial presence tests at year-end — for example a spouse living mainly in India, on a short US visit, or otherwise still filing as NRA. Also relevant when one spouse becomes resident mid-year and the other remains NRA. Dual-income or single-earner couples who want married-filing-jointly brackets, standard deduction, and credits that need a joint return should model this election carefully against the cost of taxing the NRA spouse’s worldwide (including India) income.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Attach a statement signed by both spouses to the first-year joint return declaring that on the last day of the tax year one spouse was neither a US citizen nor a §7701(b) resident and the other was, and that you choose to be treated as US residents for the entire year; include name, address, and TIN for each spouse. Check the Form 1040 Filing Status checkbox and enter the nonresident spouse’s name. You must file jointly in the election year; later years can be joint or separate while the choice remains in effect. The NRA spouse needs an SSN or ITIN (Form W-7 if ineligible for SSN). For FICA/Medicare withholding the nonresident spouse may still be treated as nonresident even while the income-tax election applies. You can also make the choice on a timely joint Form 1040-X amended return.

sections.heading: India-angle: worldwide income + treaty tradeoffs
sections.body: After the election, India salary, rental income, capital gains, and bank interest generally become US-reportable, with Form 1116 foreign tax credit often the main relief for Indian income tax paid. While the choice is in effect, neither spouse can usually claim tax-treaty benefits as a resident of India (saving-clause exceptions may still cover narrow items — see the treaty and Pub. 519). Ending or revoking the choice (revocation, death, legal separation, or IRS inadequate-records termination) generally bars either spouse from making this election again in any later year — even with a different partner. Suspension is different: if neither spouse is a US citizen/resident at any time in a later year, the choice pauses that year and both file as nonresidents if required.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: Before next filing season, list both spouses’ year-end residency status under the green card and substantial presence tests, estimate the NRA spouse’s India-source income that would enter the US return, and compare MFJ tax + Form 1116 FTC versus filing without the election (often MFS or HoH only if you qualify for a qualifying person other than the NRA spouse). If you elect, prepare the signed statement and get an ITIN/SSN for the NRA spouse in time.

cards.title: Coding agents: short AGENTS.md, hooks, fresh review
cards.body: Pulumi’s Sep 21 research roundup: keep root agent instructions short and concrete, put must-run checks in hooks (not chat), restart instead of compacting policies away, and never let the writer model grade its own diff. Directly useful for multi-agent crew ops.
cards.source: Pulumi Blog · Engin Diri · Sep 21, 2026

detail.summary: On Sep 21, 2026 Pulumi’s Engin Diri published a research-checked set of ten tips for any coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.). The through-line: move durable rules out of chat into files, hooks, tests, and fresh sessions — because compaction and long transcripts quietly drop the policies you thought were sticky. For a multi-agent crew this is ops hygiene, not a tool recommendation. Educational productivity note only.

sections.heading: Why this lands for the captain
sections.body: Your crew already leans on AGENTS.md locks, exclusive skills, and Firstmate handoffs. The Pulumi piece (plus the same week’s plan-first essays) says the win is not “prompt harder” — it is treating instruction files like code, forcing must-run checks outside the model’s choice, and separating plan → implement → review so one poisoned context cannot approve its own mistakes.

sections.heading: Instruction hygiene (tips 1–4)
sections.body: Write instructions concrete enough to verify (“API handlers live in src/api/handlers/”), not vibe-level (“keep files organized”). Treat AGENTS.md like code that rots: ~1 in 4 sampled repos had stale paths/functions in agent configs, and most AI config files are committed once then abandoned. Keep the root file short (Anthropic targets under ~200 lines); move occasional workflows into skills. Do not trust /compact to preserve safety or standing rules — research saw safety instructions collapse after repeated compaction; restart with a handoff note you wrote yourself.

sections.heading: Determinism + cost (tips 5–8)
sections.body: Hooks beat polite requests for anything that must always happen (tests, secret scans, destructive-command blocks). Do not escalate to a bigger model mid-transcript — AWS SWE-bench runs recovered more by restarting the strong model on disk state than by handing over the full poisoned chat. Count subagent tokens (multi-agent can be ~7–15× a normal session). Skip the “coordinator agent that talks a lot” pattern; give each interface an owner in a file and collect results from self-contained tasks.

sections.heading: Verify, then stop (tips 9–10 + plan-first)
sections.body: Decide the check command before the first line of code, and review in a fresh session so the writer is not grading itself. Commit on green — forced extra revisions after a passing patch often made small models worse. Same week (Sep 25–26), practitioners are converging on the same meta-move: iterate the plan until it is solid, then generate once. If you are on prompt #3 about the same block, write that block yourself.

bullets: Root AGENTS.md: short, concrete, verified — prune or it burns context and adherence
Instruction files rot; drift-check paths/scripts like you would dead links in docs
/compact can drop policies; prefer /clear + a human handoff note
Must-run steps belong in hooks (tests, secret scan), not “please remember” chat
Mid-task model upgrades with full transcript underperform a clean restart
Subagents and agent teams multiply tokens — decide delegation before spawn
Writer ≠ reviewer: fresh-context review after real tests/build
Commit when green; stop revising once checks pass
Plan-first: lock the plan before code generation (same-week practitioner echo)

On the next non-trivial task: write a one-page plan (outcome, invariants, out-of-scope, verify command), implement against it, then review the diff in a fresh session before merge.

cards.title: No US–India Social Security Totalization pact (yet)
cards.body: Unlike ~30 countries with SSA Totalization agreements, India is still not on SSA’s in-force list. Cross-border US↔India work can mean dual Social Security/EPF-style contributions with no certificate-of-coverage escape hatch, and you generally cannot combine India credits toward US quarters of coverage. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: SSA · International Agreements overview · Status of Totalization Agreements

detail.summary: The United States has bilateral Social Security “Totalization” agreements with dozens of countries. Those pacts do two jobs: (1) stop dual Social Security taxation when the same earnings would otherwise be taxed by both countries, and (2) let workers combine (“totalize”) coverage credits so a split US/foreign career can still qualify for benefits. India is not on SSA’s official list of agreements in force (as of Sep 26, 2026 — Romania entered Sep 1, 2026; India is still absent). Negotiations have been discussed for years, but until an agreement enters into force there is no SSA Certificate of Coverage path to exempt one side, and India work credits generally do not count toward US insured status. Educational only; not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin US residents and citizens who (a) work in the US while an India employer still remits EPF/social-security-style contributions, (b) are seconded US↔India on H-1B/L-1/intra-company moves, (c) are US tax residents self-employed or employed in India and still face US Social Security/self-employment tax rules, or (d) expect a career split between the two systems and assume credits will “add up” the way they do under Totalization countries. Also useful for HR/comp teams planning India assignments for US payroll employees.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Without a Totalization agreement, each country’s domestic coverage rules apply independently. US law generally covers employees for services performed in the United States regardless of citizenship or how short the stay, and it can also reach US citizens/residents working abroad for American employers (and self-employed US citizens/residents abroad). India-side EPF or other social-security contributions may still be due under Indian rules for the same period. Agreement countries use Certificates of Coverage so only one system taxes a temporary assignment; that tool does not exist for India↔US today. Separately, Totalization benefit rules that let SSA count foreign coverage toward the usual ~40 quarters for retirement insurance do not apply to India coverage.

sections.heading: India-angle: dual cost + benefit gaps
sections.body: H-1B/L-1 and other temporary India→US workers often pay full US FICA while also (or previously) funding India EPF — and may leave the US before earning enough US quarters for a US retirement benefit, with no Totalization bridge. US citizens/green-card holders on India assignments can face the mirror problem: US coverage continuing while India contributions also apply. Do not assume an EPFO Certificate of Coverage helps with US SSA the way it does for India’s agreements with Germany, Japan, Canada, etc. Watch news on a future US–India pact, but plan benefits and dual-tax exposure under current law until SSA lists India as in force.

sections.heading: What Totalization would change (if India joins)
sections.body: If a US–India agreement later enters into force, typical US Totalization features would likely include a territoriality rule, a temporary “detached worker” exemption (often up to five years) documented by Certificates of Coverage, and mutual credit totalization for benefit eligibility. Until then, none of those SSA tools apply to India. This card is educational only — employers and individuals should confirm payroll withholding and benefit projections with qualified advisors.

bullets: US Totalization agreements eliminate dual Social Security tax and can totalize coverage credits
India is NOT on SSA’s in-force agreements list (checked Sep 26, 2026)
No Certificate of Coverage path to pick only US or only India coverage for the same work
India EPF / social-security credits generally do not count toward US quarters of coverage
US FICA usually applies to work performed in the US; special rules can reach US persons abroad
Romania entered force Sep 1, 2026 — India still pending years of talks
Educational only — not tax, payroll, or benefits advice

If you have a US↔India assignment or dual payroll, ask HR/payroll which side withholds US FICA (or SE tax) and which remits India EPF/other contributions for the same months.
Pull your Social Security Statement (ssa.gov) and count US quarters of coverage — do not assume India work years will fill gaps toward the usual 40-quarter retirement insured status.

cards.title: Guardrails at every tool hop, not just the final reply
cards.body: Agentic chains call tools before the model ever answers. Put Bedrock Guardrails on AgentCore Gateway (via Policy) so every tools/call input and output is checked for prompt injection, PII, and harmful content — then keep model-layer Guardrails as a second line.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · Jun 25, 2026 · Agentic AI Lens

detail.summary: RAG could survive a single Guardrails checkpoint on the final model response. Agentic apps discover schemas, run SQL, retrieve KB chunks, and call other agents before any final answer — so a poisoned tool result can steer the next hop before the model ever speaks. The Jun 25, 2026 AWS ML Blog (data-mesh agent architecture) and Agentic AI Lens AGENTSEC08-BP01 push the same SA move: enforce Amazon Bedrock Guardrails through AgentCore Policy at the Gateway on every authorized tools/call, not only at Converse/inference. Pair that with JWT interceptors and Lake Formation for authz. Educational pattern brief — not a capacity claim.

sections.heading: Why model-only Guardrails leave a blind spot
sections.body: In a classic retrieve-then-generate flow, filtering the final model output catches most policy breaks. In an agent loop, the model may call get_schema, run_query, and kb_search several times. Indirect prompt injection living in a retrieved PDF, API payload, or tool response can influence the next tool choice before any assistant message is produced. A guardrail that only sees the final reply never sees those intermediate hops.

sections.heading: Gateway as the unified enforcement point
sections.body: AgentCore Gateway already centralizes MCP tool discovery, OAuth, and Cedar/Policy checks. When Guardrails are attached through the AgentCore Policy Engine, they evaluate inputs and outputs of every gateway target (tools, agents, models) in real time. Prompt attacks, denied topics, and sensitive-information filters can block or redact at the tool boundary, outside agent code. Keep ApplyGuardrail / Converse Guardrails at the model boundary as defense in depth — complementary, not either/or.

sections.heading: Fit with the governed data-mesh stack
sections.body: The blog’s reference customer-service agent sits on AgentCore Runtime, talks MCP through Gateway interceptors (JWT scope on request; tool-list filter + redaction on response), and reaches S3 Tables / Athena / Lake Formation plus a Bedrock Knowledge Base. Guardrails at Gateway closes the content-safety layer next to interceptor authz. For Managed Knowledge Bases you can drop a custom kb_search Lambda and use the native Gateway KB target — Policy and Guardrails still apply.

sections.heading: AGENTSEC08: validate every input surface
sections.body: Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens AGENTSEC08-BP01 says map all surfaces (user messages, tool outputs, inter-agent messages, retrieved content, memory reads) and put validation on each. The commonly missed one is external retrieval: apply Guardrails with prompt-attack detection to RAG/web/API content before it enters context. Prefer block mode for prompt attacks; use detect mode + confidence scores for softer content filters when the app can decide. When calling ApplyGuardrail yourself, set outputScope=full and ship assessments to CloudWatch — they are not auto-published.

sections.heading: Blog-ready angle for your Bedrock series
sections.body: Frame the piece as ‘Guardrails moved from the chat reply to the tool bus.’ Contrast single-checkpoint RAG with multi-hop agents, show a poisoned tool-output scenario, then diagram Gateway Policy + Guardrails beside Cedar and Lake Formation. End with a verify checklist: tools/list scope filter, blocked prompt-attack on a kb_search payload, and model-layer Guardrails still on for the final turn.

cards.title: AgentCore Runtime V2: ~2s cold starts, pay for used memory
cards.body: Next-gen Bedrock AgentCore Runtime (GA Sep 18): elastic memory reclaim + snapshot restores keep P75 cold starts ~1.9–2.0s from 200 MB–2 GB images (vs 5.4–30s on V1). Set platformVersion=V2. Strong SA cost/latency angle for production agents.
cards.source: AWS What's New · ML Blog · Sep 18, 2026

detail.summary: On Sep 18, 2026 AWS made the next-generation AgentCore Runtime generally available inside Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — the serverless microVM compute layer for production agents. Two SA-relevant wins: (1) elastic memory that starts small, pages in on demand, and reclaims cold memory so you bill for actual usage instead of the session peak; (2) snapshot-based cold starts that stay consistently ~2 seconds across 200 MB–2 GB container images, versus 5.4–30 seconds on V1. Enable with platformVersion=V2 in us-east-1, us-east-2, us-west-2, eu-west-1, and ap-northeast-1. Educational architecture note — not a capacity plan.

sections.heading: Why this matters for an SA
sections.body: Production agents are no longer short chat turns: they run minutes to hours, spike memory, and get triggered in bursts. V1 held allocated memory until the session ended (you paid the high watermark) and cold-start latency grew with image size and concurrency. V2 closes both gaps without you building spare warm pools yourself — undifferentiated heavy lifting AWS is now absorbing in the platform.

sections.heading: Elastic memory (bill the curve, not the peak)
sections.body: Each session starts with a small resident footprint. More memory is allocated as the workload touches it; when buffers are released or caches go cold, the runtime reclaims that memory instead of holding it until session end. AWS notes a higher per-GB rate but far fewer GB-hours for most agents, so the bill typically drops. Consumption pricing stays; a committed baseline option (reserve a memory floor, burst above it) is listed as coming soon for steady always-on sessions.

sections.heading: Consistent ~2s cold starts via snapshots
sections.body: On create/update, AgentCore boots your container once, waits for healthy, and snapshots the running environment (one-time init like model artifacts and static config already done). New instances restore that snapshot instead of repeating boot+init. Snapshots are stripped of transient caches so size stays roughly flat as the image grows. AWS echo-agent tests (5,000 cold invocations, client in us-west-2 calling us-east-1, no VPC peering): P75 cold start ~1.9–2.0s from 200 MB to 2 GB images vs ~5.4s–~30s on V1. Tip for interactive agents: start the session when the user opens chat, not when they hit send, so warm-up overlaps typing.

sections.heading: Regions, enablement, roadmap
sections.body: Available now in us-east-1, us-east-2, us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-northeast-1. Set platformVersion to V2 when creating or updating a runtime. Coming soon called out in the ML blog: baseline pricing discounts, larger RAM/vCPU/storage, x86 microVMs, suspend/resume with memory snapshotting, and session-scoped identity for unattended agents.

cards.title: AOTC: up to $2,500 per college student (Form 8863)
cards.body: American Opportunity Tax Credit: up to $2,500 per eligible undergrad (40% refundable). For 2026, you, a joint spouse, and the student generally need a work-authorized SSN — ITIN alone usually will not work. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Education credits (AOTC/LLC) · Form 8863 · Pub. 970

detail.summary: The American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) can cut your US tax by up to $2,500 per eligible student for the first four years of postsecondary education: 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000. Up to 40% of the credit ($1,000) can be refundable. Claim it on Form 8863 with Form 1040. MAGI phases out between $80,000–$90,000 (single/HoH) or $160,000–$180,000 (MFJ); no credit above those ceilings. Beginning with tax year 2026, new Social Security number rules apply. Educational only; not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin US residents (citizens, green-card holders, and other US tax residents) paying US or eligible foreign college tuition for themselves, a spouse (joint return), or a dependent claimed on the return — especially families with kids in the first four years of undergrad. Also relevant for recent immigrants who still hold only an ITIN: the 2026 SSN rules can block the credit until work-authorized SSNs are in place.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Student must be enrolled at least half-time for at least one academic period beginning in the tax year (or early next year if expenses were paid this year), pursuing a degree or recognized credential, and must not have completed four years of postsecondary education or already used AOTC for four tax years. Qualified expenses include tuition, required fees, and course materials needed for study (even if bought off-campus). Scholarships that reduce tuition reduce the base. You generally need Form 1098-T from the school (exceptions exist; keep enrollment and payment proof). Do not claim AOTC and the Lifetime Learning Credit for the same student in the same year.

sections.heading: India-angle: 2026 SSN rule + NRA traps
sections.body: For 2026 returns, IRS guidance says you or your joint-filing spouse and the student (if a dependent) must have a Social Security number that is valid for work and issued before the return due date (including extensions). An ITIN alone generally will not satisfy the new rule — plan ahead if a spouse or college-age dependent is still on ITIN-only status. Separately, if you (or your spouse) were a nonresident alien for any part of the year and did not elect to be treated as a US resident for tax purposes, you cannot claim education credits (Pub. 519). Married filing separately is ineligible.

sections.heading: Amounts and phaseouts
sections.body: Max credit $2,500 per eligible student. Phaseout: MAGI $80k–$90k (single/HoH/QSS) or $160k–$180k (MFJ); zero credit at or above the top of those ranges. Up to 40% of the allowed AOTC can refund even with little tax liability (subject to under-age-24 / support exceptions in the Form 8863 instructions).

cards.title: Keep LOB data home; federate tools through one Gateway
cards.body: Platform account runs the agent + Bedrock inference; each LOB keeps data in its own account and exposes MCP tools. AgentCore Gateway is the single authenticated hub — Cedar Policy + Guardrails sit outside the agent code.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · Sep 24, 2026

detail.summary: Enterprises want agents that reason across many AWS accounts without copying datasets into a shared lake. The Sep 24, 2026 AWS ML Blog walks an Expert (400) pattern: a platform account owns AgentCore Runtime + Bedrock inference + AgentCore Gateway; each line-of-business (LOB) account packages its data as an MCP server on AgentCore Runtime. Only query-time tool results cross the boundary. For SA blogs: this is the hub-and-spoke story that pairs with your prior Gateway rate-limit, managed-KB, and Guardrails cards.

sections.heading: Why single-account agents stall in the enterprise
sections.body: Each LOB keeps data in its own account for ownership, blast-radius isolation, and independent deploys. An agent that only sees one account’s DynamoDB or Knowledge Base is weak; the usual fixes — replicate everything to a hub, or weave brittle cross-account IAM into the agent — fight that model. Goal: data stays where it lives; only the specific result a tool produces flows to the platform at query time.

sections.heading: Three layers: platform, LOB spokes, Gateway hub
sections.body: Platform account: Strands (or any) agent on AgentCore Runtime, Bedrock FM access, one Guardrails config for PII/content, and AgentCore Gateway as the only MCP endpoint the agent talks to. LOB accounts: FastMCP servers on AgentCore Runtime wrapping DynamoDB lookups, Knowledge Base retrieve, or APIs — not raw S3/KB ARNs exposed to the agent. Gateway: registers each LOB MCP server as a target, does semantic tools/list across LOBs, AgentCore Identity OAuth M2M outbound, and Policy in AgentCore (Cedar) on the inbound user JWT before the call leaves the hub.

sections.heading: Identity chain that actually authorizes people
sections.body: User JWT (Okta / Cognito / Entra) reaches the agent via Runtime request headers; the agent forwards Authorization to the Gateway. Cedar evaluates permit/forbid on tool actions (e.g. allow get_balance for all authenticated users, forbid delete_customer always) — default-deny. On permit, Gateway pulls M2M credentials from AgentCore Identity and calls the LOB Runtime. Harden LOB Runtime with customJWTAuthorizer plus allowedWorkloadConfiguration tied to the Gateway ARN so callers cannot bypass Cedar by hitting the LOB MCP URL directly. Prefer OBO token exchange when the LOB tool itself needs row-level user identity; the sample uses M2M when the IdP lacks OBO.

sections.heading: Operate like a platform, not a one-off demo
sections.body: Onboard a new LOB by adding a Gateway target — agent rediscovers tools on the next tools/list. Use AgentCore Evaluations online (sample live traffic for Tool Selection Accuracy / Correctness / Goal Success Rate) and on-demand dataset eval in CI so what you gate matches what you monitor. Attribute platform Bedrock/Gateway spend back to LOBs with cost-allocation tags on the agent role plus tool-trace counts; LOB data-plane costs already land in each spoke account. For production networking, move off public Runtime mode to VPC ENIs + PrivateLink ingress to Gateway.

sections.heading: Blog angle for Solutions Architects
sections.body: Lead with “data gravity, not agent gravity”: diagram platform vs LOB vs Gateway, then the JWT → Cedar → M2M → LOB path. Contrast wrapping a standalone Knowledge Base inside the LOB MCP server (fine control) vs attaching a Managed Knowledge Base as a native Gateway connector (less DIY). Tie to your earlier cards: Gateway rate limits / Dogwood for cost abuse, InvokeGuardrailChecks for per-step content scores, Gateway Cedar for tool authorization. Close with the decision table: centralize inference + policy; distribute data + tool implementation.

cards.body: BlackRock MUB (~$1.2B) and Vanguard VTEB (~$1.7B) posted their largest weekly inflows ever as tax-exempt yields jumped. For an ETF-first sleeve, this is a tax-equivalent yield story — educational only, not a trade signal.

detail.summary: On 24 Sep 2026, Bloomberg reported that the two largest US municipal-bond ETFs — iShares National Muni Bond ETF (MUB) and Vanguard Tax-Exempt Bond Index ETF (VTEB) — recorded their largest weekly inflows ever (~$1.2B and ~$1.7B). For US taxable investors, muni income is generally federal-tax-exempt (and often state-exempt for in-state bonds), so the relevant comparison is tax-equivalent yield versus Treasuries or corporates — not the raw SEC yield alone. Educational only; not investment or tax advice.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: After rising Treasury rates and heavy new muni issuance pressured prices, investors poured record weekly cash into the two largest national tax-exempt bond ETFs. Vanguard’s Nathan Will framed it as attractive tax-equivalent yields plus better valuations versus taxable bonds; some strategists also pointed to tax-loss harvesting swaps after the rout. Separate CNBC coverage (18 Sep) noted investment-grade munis offering high tax-equivalent yields for top brackets versus Treasuries/corporates, with MUB cited as a low-cost (~0.05% ER) national IG vehicle.

sections.heading: Why it maps to an ETF-first plan
sections.body: If the core portfolio is professional-managed funds rather than individual bond picking, national muni bond ETFs are the usual way to get diversified, liquid, tax-exempt fixed income without assembling a ladder of individual CUSIPs. Record ETF inflows are a flow/sentiment datapoint — they do not by themselves prove future returns. Rate risk remains: longer-duration munis move more when yields rise further.

sections.heading: India-origin / US tax angle

State tax treatment depends on fund holdings and your state of residence — a national ETF like MUB/VTEB is mostly federal-exempt; in-state exemption usually needs a state-specific fund. This is not a substitute for advice on Form 1099-INT / Schedule B reporting or AMT nuances.

A single record week into MUB/VTEB after a selloff can reflect rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting, or bargain hunting — not a green light to concentrate. Size any fixed-income sleeve to risk tolerance and time horizon; prefer understanding duration and credit quality over FOMO on flow headlines.

cards.title: QCD: give from your IRA tax-free up to $111k (2026)
cards.body: If you are 70½+, a Qualified Charitable Distribution lets your IRA trustee pay a US-eligible charity directly — up to $111,000 excluded from income in 2026, and it can cover your RMD. India NGOs usually do not qualify. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Notice 2025-67 · Pub. 590-B · IRA FAQs

detail.summary: A Qualified Charitable Distribution (QCD) is a direct transfer from your traditional IRA (not an ongoing SEP/SIMPLE) to a US organization eligible to receive deductible charitable contributions. You must be at least age 70½ when the distribution is made. For tax year 2026, Notice 2025-67 raises the annual exclusion from $108,000 to $111,000 per IRA owner (spouse can use a separate $111,000 on a joint return). A proper QCD is excluded from gross income, can satisfy all or part of your required minimum distribution (RMD), and is not also claimed as a charitable deduction. Educational only; not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin US residents (and US-person parents) age 70½+ with traditional IRA balances who already give to charity, who face RMDs, or who want to keep adjusted gross income lower for Medicare IRMAA, Social Security taxation, or credit phase-outs. Also useful for adult children helping parents coordinate custodian paperwork before year-end.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: The IRA trustee must pay the charity directly (a check you deposit yourself usually fails the QCD rules). Keep the same written acknowledgment you would need for a deductible gift (Pub. 526). On Form 1040, report the full IRA distribution, enter $0 (or the taxable remainder) as the taxable amount, and write QCD next to that line. If the IRA has basis (nondeductible contributions) or you have other IRA distributions the same year, Form 8606 may still be required — see the IRS IRA FAQs.

sections.heading: India-angle trap
sections.body: QCDs must go to US-qualified charities (generally §501(c)(3) organizations that can receive deductible contributions). Temples, NGOs, or family trusts in India almost never qualify for a QCD, even if the cause is worthy. For India-side giving, other tools (after-tax gifts, US dual-qualified charities, or non-QCD strategies) apply — do not assume a remittance to India counts as a QCD.

sections.heading: Limits and one-time SIE election
sections.body: Annual QCD exclusion for 2026: $111,000 under §408(d)(8)(A). Excess above that is taxable like a normal distribution. Separately, a one-time election can send up to $55,000 (2026; was $54,000) to certain split-interest entities (CRAT/CRUT/charitable gift annuity) funded only by QCDs — see Notice 2025-67 and Pub. 590-B. QCDs count toward RMDs but do not create a double charitable deduction.

Excluded from income — do not also deduct as a charitable contribution
India NGOs / temples usually do not qualify — need US-eligible charity
Report on Form 1040 with “QCD”; Form 8606 may still apply

cards.title: Design the room; stop waiting for motivation
cards.body: James Clear: environment is the invisible hand on habits. Make good cues obvious and bad ones hard to reach — self-control becomes less about grit.
cards.source: James Clear · Atomic Habits (via lijubjohn notes)

detail.summary: Atomic Habits argues that motivation is overrated and environment is underrated. You are less a consumer of willpower than a designer of cues: put good-habit triggers in plain sight, remove bad-habit triggers, and reduce the steps between you and the behavior you want. When the room does the reminding, you need less heroics.

sections.heading: Environment beats pep talks
sections.body: Clear’s notes frame environment as the invisible hand that shapes behavior. Similar people act differently when the room changes — snacks on the counter vs. in a hard-to-reach cupboard, phone on the nightstand vs. charging outside the bedroom. Self-control is easier when the right action is the path of least resistance, not when you white-knuckle through a bad setup every day.

sections.heading: Make good habits obvious (and easy)
sections.body: Law 1 (Make It Obvious) and Law 3 (Make It Easy) meet here: design cues you can see, then prime the space so the next step is short. Leave the book on the pillow, the running shoes by the door, the water bottle filled on the desk. Reduce friction — fewer steps between you and the habit — and prime tomorrow’s environment tonight so future-you does not negotiate.

sections.heading: Make bad habits invisible (and hard)
sections.body: The inverse laws: hide or remove cues (Make It Invisible) and add steps (Make It Difficult). Logout of distracting apps, move junk food off the counter, put the TV remote in another room. Commitment devices — rules that constrain future choices — turn a one-time design decision into ongoing protection so you are not relying on 9 p.m. willpower.

sections.heading: Architect, don’t just consume
sections.body: The punchline in the notes: be the designer of your world, not merely the consumer of it. A stable setup where everything has a place and a purpose makes habits easier to form. Pick one context you live in daily (desk, kitchen, phone home screen) and redesign it so the default action is the smart one.

Reduce friction for good habits; add friction for bad ones

cards.title: Cursor Projects: one coordinator for long-lived agent work
cards.body: Cursor launched Projects (Sep 10): a coordinator agent that keeps shared context for months, fans out cloud subagents, and can subscribe to Slack/PRs/schedules. Built for features, migrations, and ongoing “gardening” — not one-shot chats. Educational ops note.

detail.summary: On Sep 10, 2026 Cursor shipped Projects in beta. A Project is a long-lived body of work (feature, migration, or standing job) directed through one coordinator agent. The coordinator does not write code itself — it delegates to many cloud (and when needed local) agents, keeps shared context that grows over months, and can act on subscriptions (Slack, schedules, PR events) without waiting for a fresh prompt. Cursor reports new users merge ~30% more PRs; heavy Projects users merge about 6× as many. Educational productivity note — not a product endorsement or purchase advice.

sections.heading: What changed vs a normal chat
sections.body: Chats are short-lived and amnesiac across sessions. A Project owns durable shared files that sync to every machine its agents use: research, artifacts, repo learnings, and how you prefer work done. If one agent figures out how to test a service, later agents reuse those instructions. That moves the unit of work up from “one prompt” to “a body of work that outlives a single session.”

sections.heading: Coordinator pattern (why it stays responsive)
sections.body: You chat with the coordinator. It directs other agents that execute. Because it delegates instead of coding inline, it is less likely to get blocked mid-task and can keep taking direction while workers run in parallel. Cloud-by-default means closing your laptop does not stop the fleet; a local agent can still be spun up when something must run on your machine.

sections.heading: Three patterns Cursor highlights
sections.body: Feature work: research → shared context → parallel implement/test → optional local try → post-ship monitoring with the same context. Migrations: agree a safe approach once, then apply it across hundreds of PRs with declining review intensity as quality holds. Gardening: standing quality work (design-system lint, CI fixes, bug triage) driven by PR/Slack/schedule subscriptions so the coordinator acts when signals appear.

sections.heading: Why this maps to an SA / multi-agent ops lane
sections.body: If you already run orchestrator + specialist agents (or Bedrock agent fleets), Projects is the IDE-side cousin of that pattern: durable context, parallel workers, event-driven wakeups. Useful mental model even if you stay on AWS-native stacks — the product lesson is “promote work that outlives a chat into a supervised project with subscriptions,” not “buy this tool.”

cards.title: Health FSA: $3,400 pre-tax medical dollars for 2026 (not an HSA)
cards.body: Employer health Flexible Spending Arrangement lets you set aside up to $3,400 in 2026 via payroll (carryover up to $680 if the plan allows). Useful when you have predictable dental/vision/Rx costs and are NOT on an HSA-eligible HDHP. Educational only, not tax advice.

detail.summary: A health Flexible Spending Arrangement (health FSA) under a §125 cafeteria plan lets eligible employees reduce salary on a pre-tax basis and use the money for qualified medical expenses. For plan years beginning in 2026, the IRS voluntary employee salary-reduction limit is $3,400 (up $100). If the plan permits carryover of unused amounts, the maximum carryover is $680. Unlike an HSA, a general-purpose health FSA is typically use-it-or-lose-it (subject to plan grace period or carryover rules) and is aimed at people with a traditional (non-HDHP) medical plan. Educational only; not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin US employees and dual-income households on employer medical plans who can forecast recurring out-of-pocket costs (glasses, dental work, orthodontia, copays, OTC meds that qualify under plan rules). Especially helpful at open enrollment when comparing HSA+HDHP vs traditional plan + FSA.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Elect an amount at open enrollment (or hire/qualifying event). Contributions come out of paycheck before federal income tax (and usually FICA). You spend via debit card or claims for IRS-qualified medical expenses for yourself, spouse, and tax dependents. Year-end leftover balance is forfeited unless the plan offers a grace period (up to 2½ months) OR a carryover (max $680 for 2026) — plans generally offer one or the other, not both.

sections.heading: HSA conflict (important)
sections.body: You generally cannot contribute to an HSA for any month you are covered by a general-purpose health FSA (or a general-purpose HRA). Limited-purpose (dental/vision only) or post-deductible FSAs are the usual exception. If you already use an HSA (see prior tip tax-20260912), do not elect a general-purpose FSA.

sections.heading: India-angle note
sections.body: Cross-border families often underestimate US dental/vision costs relative to India pricing. An FSA turns those predictable US bills into pre-tax dollars — but only while you are on a US employer cafeteria plan.
